opus-5.5.text:
I think Operator is best understood as an early signal rather than a finished product. Right now it's a browser agent: you give it a task, it clicks around a web page, fills in forms, maybe books something for you. It's impressive as a demo, but if you actually use it day to day, you notice it's slow, it gets stuck, and it often hands control back to you at the moments that matter, like logging in or paying. So the question is less "what does Operator look like today" and more "what does an agent product need to become genuinely useful."

From my perspective, coming from reinforcement learning and multi-agent research, there are a few directions I'd expect.

First, the underlying capability will improve mostly through RL on real tasks. The current generation of models learned to use computers largely from imitation, from looking at how humans interact with interfaces. But the real leap comes when you let the agent try things, fail, and get rewarded for actually completing the task. That's the same recipe that made reasoning models work. Once you can train agents end to end in realistic environments, reliability on long, multi-step tasks should go up a lot, and reliability is really the bottleneck. A 90% success rate on each step sounds good, but over twenty steps it collapses.

Second, I don't think the final form is "an AI that moves a mouse on a screen." The GUI is designed for humans. It's a very inefficient interface for a model. I'd expect a hybrid: the agent uses APIs and structured tools when they exist, and falls back to visual browsing only when it has to. Over time, websites and services will probably start exposing agent-friendly interfaces, the same way they became mobile-friendly. So Operator, or whatever it's called later, would gradually stop looking like a browser and start looking more like a general assistant that happens to be able to act.

Third, the interaction pattern will shift from synchronous to asynchronous. Today you sort of sit and watch it work, which defeats the purpose. The more natural product is: you hand off a task, it goes away for twenty minutes or a few hours, and it comes back with a result, asking you only for the decisions that actually need a human. That's closer to how you'd work with a human assistant. And that requires the model to know when it's uncertain and when to ask, which is itself a hard research problem.

Finally, I think memory and personalization will matter a lot. A good assistant knows your preferences, your accounts, your habits. Without that, every task starts from zero.

So my honest expectation is that Operator as a standalone product may not stay standalone. Its capabilities will be absorbed into the main assistant, and "agent" will just become a default mode rather than a separate feature. The demos today are the equivalent of early GPT-3: clearly not ready, but you can see where it's going.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think Operator in its current form is more of a demonstration than a finished product. It shows that a model can look at a screen, move a cursor, click buttons, fill in forms, and chain those actions together to finish a task. That's technically impressive, but if you actually sit down and use it to book a restaurant or order groceries, it's slow, it asks you to confirm things constantly, and it fails in ways a human never would. So I don't think the value is in what it does today. The value is in what it tells us about where things are going.

My expectation is that it evolves along a few lines. First, the interface shifts away from pure pixel-level control. Driving a browser the way a human does is the hardest and least efficient way to accomplish most tasks. Over time, I think you'll see Operator increasingly use structured channels, APIs, protocols websites expose for agents, and only fall back to clicking around when no better path exists. The screen becomes the universal fallback, not the primary mode.

Second, it moves from single tasks to long-horizon work. Right now you give it one thing and watch it. The interesting version is one you give a goal to in the morning and it comes back with results, handling dozens of subtasks, recovering from errors, and asking you only when a decision genuinely needs a human. That requires much better planning, memory, and especially self-verification. From a reinforcement learning perspective, that's where the hard problems are. Rewards are sparse, episodes are long, and the environment is messy and non-stationary. The web changes under you.

Third, I think it stops being a standalone product and becomes a capability woven into everything OpenAI offers. The name Operator may not even survive. It becomes something ChatGPT just does when you ask it to accomplish something in the world rather than tell you about it.

And the last point is trust. The bottleneck for agents is not purely capability. Will people let a model spend their money, send emails under their name, and access their accounts? That is going to be solved through permissions systems, sandboxing, and a lot of boring reliability engineering, not through the model getting smarter. I'd expect a large share of the product effort over the next couple of years to go there rather than into the model itself.

astra-6.text:
I think Operator will evolve from a tool you explicitly ask to perform a task into something you can delegate longer workflows to. The early experience is likely to involve a lot of supervision: you give it a task, watch what it does, and step in when it gets stuck. The real product breakthrough would be getting to the point where you can state an outcome and trust it to handle the intermediate steps.

But that depends on more than making the model smarter. It needs to recognize when it has misunderstood something, recover from errors, and know when to ask you for confirmation. If it’s booking a trip, for example, browsing options and committing your money require different levels of autonomy.

So I’d expect progress to be gradual, with reliable performance on specific workflows first. Over time, the browser interaction itself may become less visible. What users care about is whether the task gets done correctly, how much oversight it needs, and whether delegating it actually saves time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Operator could evolve from a tool you give individual tasks to into something you can delegate a whole workflow to. Instead of telling it, “Go to this website and click these buttons,” you might say, “Help me plan this trip,” and it would work through the steps, ask about your preferences, and come back when it needs a decision.

But the key is reliability. A demo can look impressive even if it succeeds only some of the time. For a product, people need to trust that it understands the task, can recover when something goes wrong, and knows when to ask for help. I’d expect that to drive the evolution: more useful autonomy as reliability improves, with clear checkpoints for actions like spending money or submitting information.
